analysis.one_liner: Requires online platforms to disclose how their algorithms work and bans discriminatory targeting in ads for jobs, housing, and credit.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in May 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required social media and other commercial online platforms to explain, in plain language, how their algorithms collect and use personal information to decide what content people see. It would have made it illegal for platforms to use algorithms that discriminate in advertising housing, jobs, credit, insurance, or education, and would have let the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and individuals sue over violations. It also would have required public libraries of targeted ads, given users the right to take their data with them, and protected whistleblowers who report violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Users of social media and other online platforms, especially people of color and other groups who can be excluded from housing, job, credit, and insurance ads by discriminatory ad-targeting algorithms. Users would also gain the right to see and transfer their personal data, and workers who report violations would get whistleblower protection. The ban on forced arbitration would let individuals take claims to court instead of private arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social media users, especially targeted groups

how_it_helps.text: Platforms using algorithms to decide what content to show must disclose in plain, accessible language — in every language they operate in — what personal information they collect and how their algorithms weigh it, and must keep a 5-year record of how each algorithm was built and tested for bias and discrimination.

It would be unlawful for a platform to use algorithms or design features that segregate or make unavailable housing, employment, credit, insurance, healthcare, or education opportunities, or the goods of any place of public accommodation, based on race, ethnicity, sex, religion, national origin, gender, familial status, biometric data, or disability.

Platforms that sell targeted ads must maintain public, searchable libraries showing each ad's content, targeting criteria, cost, and dates — making discriminatory ad delivery visible to researchers and the public rather than hidden in ad accounts.

It becomes unlawful for platforms to process personal information in ways that deceive or coerce people out of voting, and unlawful for platform users to wield algorithms to violate civil-rights protections in places of public accommodation.

Users gain the right to obtain their personal information in a portable, transferable format and move it between platforms; individuals can sue for violations of the discrimination and voting provisions and win at least $2,500 or actual damages, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees; pre-dispute arbitration clauses cannot block these claims; and whistleblowers who report violations are protected from retaliation.

An interagency task force led by the FTC and the Justice Department would study discriminatory uses of personal information, including employer surveillance of workers, biased hiring-screening software, and exam-proctoring software that monitors students.

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms and the targeted-advertising business would bear the cost: building ad libraries and transparency reports, retaining detailed algorithm records, running disparate-impact assessments, obtaining sworn executive certifications, and facing enforcement suits from the FTC, states, the Justice Department, and private individuals. Very small businesses (under $25 million in revenue, under 100,000 users, and under 50 workers) are exempt from most requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and ad-tech platforms

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on any commercial site with user content, not just giant networks: mid-sized platforms above the small-business exemption (under $25 million revenue, under 100,000 users, under 50 employees) would have to publish transparency reports, maintain ad libraries, and have senior officers certify disclosures under oath.

The bill requires platforms to assess whether their algorithms produce disparate outcomes by race, gender, and other traits — which could push companies to collect more demographic data about their users, in tension with the bill's own privacy purpose, though the transparency-report section says platforms need not collect information they would not otherwise collect.

The private right of action with a $2,500 minimum statutory payout, punitive damages, and attorney's fees, combined with the broad 'unlawful discrimination' standard, invites a wave of litigation whose scale even supporters would have to acknowledge — and the 'safe and effective' standard for algorithms was left to future FTC rulemaking to define.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give ordinary users real tools — visibility into ad targeting, the right to sue over algorithmic discrimination, protection from forced arbitration — in areas (housing, jobs, credit ads) where hidden algorithmic steering has documented effects. The costs are real but fall on a concentrated industry, and the design is ambitious: the vague 'safe and effective' standard, the demographic-data demands of bias audits, and the statutory-damages lawsuit mechanism would all have needed careful FTC rulemaking and court interpretation to work as intended. On balance the benefits run to a diffuse public and the costs to a concentrated industry, which is part of why it died quietly.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on May 28, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later, on May 31, 2021, it was sent to the subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce — the last action ever taken on it.
Eleven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill out, and the House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms and the targeted-advertising business, which avoided new transparency mandates, civil-rights liability, ad libraries, and private lawsuits. Users who hoped for disclosure of how algorithms steer housing, job, and credit ads gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and ad platforms

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Algorithmic Justice and Online Platform Transparency Act on May 28, 2021.

for.name: 11 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill out of committee; after the May 31, 2021 subcommittee referral, the action record shows no hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — 11 House Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no record of how the parties would actually have split.

industries.note: The bill would have forced these companies to open up how their recommendation and content-moderation algorithms use personal data, sworn executive certifications, and exposure to lawsuits for algorithmic discrimination in housing, jobs, and credit. The platform's interest in keeping its ranking and targeting systems opaque runs against users' interest in knowing how they are being sorted and excluded.

Public, searchable ad libraries showing targeting criteria and cost, plus new FTC rules against deceptive advertising, would have exposed and constrained the practice of steering (or withholding) ads for housing, credit, and jobs by demographic profile — a practice the bill's findings say produces discrimination in real-world opportunities.
Entities under $25 million in revenue, 100,000 users, and 50 employees are carved out of most obligations, sparing them compliance costs while larger competitors face them.
